title: Why this program
intro: No randomized trials have compared pull-up progression schemes head to head. Linear plans, rep ladders, and rest-pause protocols in pull-ups simply have not been tested in controlled studies.

This program is a synthesis built from indirect evidence: training frequency, weekly set volume, rest between sets, how close you train to failure, autoregulated progression, and eccentric loading for beginners. Every design choice below ties back to published research.
Where data come from bench press, lat pulldown, or squat studies, we say so. Those transfers are extrapolations, not proven facts about pull-ups.

overview.title: How the program is structured
body: You start with a max-rep test. That result sets an anchor M*, your current estimate of how many strict pull-ups you can do in one set. Each workout has five sets. A cycle has six workouts, each one a step with slightly higher targets.

Sets 1 through 4 stay submaximal: fixed rep targets at 50 to 70% of your anchor. Set 5 is a max set with a minimum rep count that rises each step. Hit every target and you advance. Miss any set and you repeat the same step next time.

The anchor updates after each completed cycle and again at a formal retest every four weeks. Volume lands at 15 hard sets per week at the default three sessions [16][17]. One set per workout goes near failure for a progression signal [36][37]. Progression gates on actual performance, not a fixed calendar [28][29].

levels.title: Entry test and levels
body: On your first session you do strict pull-ups to failure. The count is M. If M is zero, you enter Path 0 (eccentric and assisted work). Otherwise the app stores M as your anchor M* and assigns a level label.

Levels are display tags only. They do not change the math. M = 0 maps to Path 0. M from 1 to 4 is L1 Beginner. M from 5 to 9 is L2 Base. M from 10 to 19 is L3 Intermediate. M 20 or more is L4 Advanced.
The label helps you read progress charts. Step targets always come from the generator rule and your current anchor, not from the level name.

algorithm.title: Step generator: session(M*, k)
body: The app does not store fixed workout tables. It generates each step from your anchor M* and the step index k (1 through 6 in the current cycle).

Working sets 1 to 4 use ceil(0.7·M*), ceil(0.6·M*), ceil(0.6·M*), ceil(0.5·M*), each at least 1 rep. Set 5 is type Maximum with minimum N_k = min(ceil(0.6·M*) + k − 1, M* + 1). The cap at M* + 1 means we never ask for more than one rep above your tested max in a single step.
Example with M* = 7 and k = 3: working targets are 5, 5, 5, 4. The final set minimum is N_3 = min(5 + 2, 8) = 7. Full reference tables for M* = 3, 7, 15, and 25 appear in the formulas section below.

progression.title: Success, failure, deload, and retest
body: Success means all five sets meet their targets, including final set reps at or above N_k. You move to step k + 1 on the next scheduled workout.

Failure means any working set falls short or the final set lands below N_k. The same step repeats. Two consecutive failures on one step trigger a deload: M* becomes floor(0.9·M*), minimum 1. The next step recalculates from the lower anchor. Autoregulated load changes perform at least as well as fixed progression in meta-analyses [28], with no significant downside in others [29]. Deload weeks are common in trained lifters, roughly every five to six weeks [32].

After six successful steps, the cycle ends. New anchor M*' = max(best final-set reps in the cycle, M* − 1). A new cycle starts at step 1. Every two cycles, about four weeks at three sessions per week, you run a full max test. That result becomes the new M*. Repeated max tests do not inflate strength gains on their own [34]. After a break longer than two weeks, the app suggests a retest or a roughly 10% anchor reduction.

frequency.title: Frequency: 3 sessions per week, 48 h minimum gap
body: Default schedule is three non-consecutive days per week, for example Monday, Wednesday, Friday. You must leave at least 48 hours between sessions.

Training a muscle group twice per week beats once per week for hypertrophy in meta-analysis [7]. For upper-body strength, three or more sessions per week beat one when weekly volume is matched [9]. Strength usually returns within about two days after a session when acute loss stays under 20% [14].
Two sessions per week is a valid option, especially at advanced levels if progress stalls. ACSM guidelines recommend training major muscle groups at least twice weekly [12].

volume.title: Volume: 5 sets × 3 workouts = 15 per week
body: Each workout has five sets. Three workouts per week gives 15 hard sets for the pulling muscles.

Strength meta-analysis finds at least 10 sets per week clearly beats five or fewer (effect size 0.18) [16]. For hypertrophy in trained people, 12 to 20 sets per week per muscle is a common optimum band [17]. A lat-pulldown trial found five sets beat three and one for both strength and rep-max performance [19].
Fifteen weekly sets sit inside that range without pushing into diminishing returns territory [18]. More volume helps up to a point, then gains flatten, especially for strength.

workingSets.title: Working sets: submaximal descending reps
body: The four working sets use descending fractions of your anchor: 70%, 60%, 60%, and 50%, rounded up. That keeps most reps away from deep failure.

Pull-up research comparing velocity-loss cutoffs found that stopping sets at 25% velocity loss produced larger strength and endurance gains than allowing 50% loss [1]. Broader failure literature shows strength gains are similar across a wide range of reps in reserve [36]. Training every set to failure costs you reps in later sets and adds soreness [42].
Submaximal front sets preserve quality for the final max set. That pattern matches what we know about managing fatigue across multiple sets.

finalMax.title: Final set: Maximum with rising minimum
body: Set 5 is always a max effort with a floor of N_k reps. N_k rises by one each step until it hits the cap M* + 1. Over a full cycle the minimum typically climbs by three reps total.

Muscle size tends to increase as sets end closer to failure, but the effect is small [36][39]. For strength, failure is not required [37][38]. Local muscular endurance gains look similar whether you stop at failure or two reps in reserve [41].

The exact protocol of four submaximal sets plus one max set has not been tested as a single package in a randomized trial. We built it from separate lines of evidence on volume, failure proximity, and autoregulation. Treat that combination as an extrapolation.

rest.title: Rest between sets: 3 min default
body: Default rest is three minutes between sets. Presets offer 90 seconds and five minutes. You can adjust in 15-second steps during a workout.

For strength, three to five minutes between sets at 50 to 90% of max allows more reps across multiple sets than shorter rest [21]. Trained lifters need more than two minutes to maximize strength gains [23]. Short rest collapses rep output: at one minute between squat sets, reps fell from 7.7 to 2.2 by set four; at five minutes they held 7.4 to 4.7 [26].

For hypertrophy, benefit from rest beyond 90 seconds is unclear. A 2024 Bayesian meta-analysis found no meaningful difference above 90 seconds [25]. A 2025 preprint argues long rest does not beat short rest for hypertrophy, though it still favors long rest for strength [27]. Our goal is rep-max performance, so three minutes stays the default. Path 0 uses 90 seconds to three minutes between sets.

path0.title: Path 0: starting from zero pull-ups
body: If your max test is zero, you follow a 12-step path across three phases, four workouts each, at three sessions per week.

Steps 1 to 4: scapular pulls 3×8–10 plus dead hangs 3×20–30 seconds, adding five seconds to hangs each step. Steps 5 to 8: negative pull-ups 3×5 with three to five second lowering plus assisted pull-ups 3×6–8. Steps 9 to 12: negatives 3×6 plus assisted 3×8. Then you retest and enter L1 if you can do at least one rep.

Eccentric training has the strongest evidence for building strength when concentric max is limited [43][44]. Eccentric-only work beats concentric-only for eccentric strength, but concentric strength needs concentric practice too [46]. A 12-week pull-up program with controlled eccentric tempo raised max reps from 2.1 to 7.8 in one trial [2]. Scapular pulls and hang progressions lack direct RCTs. Those phases are coaching practice, marked as extrapolation.

skips.title: Missed workouts and return after a break
body: Skipping a scheduled day does not advance or penalize your step. The missed workout stays available. Later dates shift forward by the gap while keeping the same spacing between sessions.

Strength is maintained for up to about three weeks without training, then decays faster [48]. Adolescent athletes showed no loss after three weeks off [51]. A break of two weeks or less: resume the same step. Longer breaks: take a fresh max test or accept an automatic anchor cut.

Flexible scheduling supports long-term exercise habits better than rigid time windows in a large field experiment [49]. Guilt after a missed session correlates with worse outcomes in relapse-prevention research [50]. The calendar marks skipped days neutrally, not in red.

rejected.title: Patterns we rejected
body: Daily high-frequency training without rest days conflicts with recovery data. Strength typically returns within two days, which implies spacing hard sessions at least 48 hours apart [14].

Very high weekly volumes with no deload or performance gate risk overuse and ignore dose-response ceilings [16][17]. Rest-pause protocols have RCT support on bench press and curls, not on pull-ups [6]. With fixed bodyweight load, the main rest-pause benefit (more reps at the same external load) matters less.
We do not use an RPE or reps-in-reserve scale in the UI. Novices mis-estimate effort by more than a rep on average [30]. The app uses an objective pass or fail gate instead.

limitations.title: Honest limits
body: No RCT has tested this exact progression scheme in pull-ups. Most evidence is transferred from other exercises or muscle groups.
The four-plus-one max set structure, Path 0 hang and scapular progressions, and skip-reschedule policy are project extrapolations, not replicated trial findings.

Literature disagrees on some details. Training frequency at matched volume [7][13], autoregulation versus fixed loading [28][29], and long versus short rest for hypertrophy [25][27] all have conflicting papers. We picked conservative defaults aimed at rep-max gains and note the disputes where they matter.
